function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run manually) to finish the task.  
All the files that need to be added to the repo are shown in full – just create them in the appropriate locations and commit/push.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with  
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

The repo contains a very small Node.js app (`index.js` + `package.json`).  
A minimal, production‑ready Dockerfile looks like this:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Use the official Node.js 18 slim image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /app

# Install only production dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
```

> **Why `node:18-alpine`?**  
> Alpine is tiny, the latest LTS (18.x) is stable, and it keeps the image size down.

> **What about `npm start`?**  
> The repo’s `package.json` already defines `"start": "node index.js"`, so `CMD ["node", "index.js"]` is equivalent.

> **Add a `.dockerignore`** (recommended):

```
node_modules
npm-debug.log
.git
.gitignore
Dockerfile
.dockerignore
```

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a single file `k8s.yaml` (or split into `deployment.yaml` & `service.yaml` – both work).

```yaml
# k8s.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # change if you use another registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # external port
    targetPort: 3000  # container port
```

> **What this does**  
> * 2 replicas of the pod  
> * Exposes the app on port 3000 inside the pod  
> * Creates a ClusterIP service that forwards traffic from port 80 to the pods

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions – CI workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows` if it doesn’t exist, then add `ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v3

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v2
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v4
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
```

> **What it does**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`  
> * Builds the Docker image from the repo root  
> * Pushes the image to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`) under the same name as the repo

> **Prerequisites**  
> * No extra secrets are required – the workflow uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN`.  
> * If you prefer Docker Hub or another registry, replace the login and tag lines accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile .dockerignore k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After the push, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run, build the image, and push it to the registry.

---

### Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify Dockerfile builds locally
docker build -t nodejs-welcome:local .

# Run the container
docker run -p 3000:3000 nodejs-welcome:local
# Visit http://localhost:3000 in your browser – you should see the “Hello World” response

# Apply the Kubernetes manifests (if you have a cluster)
kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml
```

That’s it! 🎉  
You now have a fully containerised Node.js app, ready for deployment on Kubernetes, and a CI pipeline that automatically builds and publishes the image whenever you push to `main`.
